new_statements.quote: One of these is Kugu Nganhcara, a Pama-Nyungan language of Australia, as described by Smith & Johnson (2000). In this language, with consonants /p, t, t̪, c, k, b, d, d̪, j, g, m, n, n̪, ɲ, ŋ, l, r, w, j/, all consonants except the tap, /r/, have geminate allophones optionally in intervocalic position following a short initial stressed syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand and indirect: Smith & Johnson's (2000) description of Kugu Nganhcara, as relayed by Blevins, treats the word-initial syllable as the stressed syllable (optional gemination of a following consonant when that initial stressed syllable is short). Consistent first-hand evidence seen only in snippets: Smith 1986:517 says traditional (Edward River) Kugu Muminh is 'syllable-timed' but with initial syllables c. 20% longer than non-initial ones (Johnson 1974), while younger Aurukun Muminh speakers, under Wik Mungkan influence, show 'stress-timed' pronunciation with rhythmically strong (stressed) initial syllables and reduction of medial/final short vowels. Provisional reading: word-initial prominence/stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the accessible text. (Smith & Johnson 1986:36 note the long/short vowel contrast is 'generally restricted to initial syllables'; enclitic pronouns are prosodically dependent per Klavans 1985 snippet.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, as presupposed in an allophony statement; no discussion of phrase stress or citation forms available. Statement is about Kugu Nganhcara as a whole (all six patrilects share phonology with 'only minor' differences, Smith & Johnson 1986:34-36); nothing exists for Kugu Mangk specifically.
new_statements.identity_note: kuku1279 'Kuku-Mangk' is a retired Glottolog bookkeeping entry (ISO xmq): no form-meaning pairs of Kugu Mangk have ever been recorded; Glottolog redirects it to Wik-Iiyanh [wij] (wiki1239). Smith & Johnson (1986:30-31; 2000:358 as cited by Sutton & Hale 2021:83 fn.8) regard Kugu Mangk as probably an alternative label for Kugu Yi'anh, one of the six mutually intelligible Kugu Nganhcara patrilects (Glottolog Wikngenchera wikn1246 with dialect-level entries kuku1280 Kuku-Uwanh [WALS knc], kuku1283 Kuku-Muminh, kuku1282 Kuku-Mu'inh, kuku1281 Kuku-Ugbanh, wiki1239 Wik-Iiyanh); von Sturmer 1978:171 reports some people treat it as distinct. Everything quoted here concerns Kugu Nganhcara as a whole (Blevins <- Smith & Johnson 2000) or Kugu Muminh specifically (Smith 1986 = kuku1283). Any catalog entry should be filed under the Kugu Nganhcara languoid, not under kuku1279.
